extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians, geometers, and advanced mathematics students (readers of a 19th-century mathematical journal)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and criteria for identifying and classifying second-order surfaces (quadrics) by reducing a general second-order equation to primitive canonical forms; includes an algorithm (complete-the-square) and a criterion for surfaces of revolution. Also contains related geometric formulae (tetrahedron radii, circumradius, and some solution methods for cubics and perturbation of planetary elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive form mapping to species of second-order surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: A general second-order equation in x,y,z may be identified with one of a set of primitive forms; each primitive form corresponds to a particular species (ellipsoid, hyperboloid, paraboloid, cylinder, cone, two planes, pair of parallel planes, straight line, imaginary surface, etc.). The page lists primitive forms (numbered (1) to (8)) and the species corresponding to sign/parameter conditions (e.g., form (1) x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = a denotes an ellipsoid when a>0; other sign combinations and degenerate constants give hyperboloids, cones, cylinders, two planes, imaginary, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the table of primitive forms and the sign/parameter conditions provided to classify the quadric once it has been brought to one of the primitive forms. The page explicitly enumerates cases (ellipsoid, hyperboloid of one or two sheets, elliptic/hyperbolic/parabolic cylinders, cones, pair of planes, two parallel planes, straight line, imaginary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm: reduce general quadratic to primitive form by successive completing-the-square
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the general second-order equation as x^2 + P(y,z)x + Q(y,z) = 0 with P linear in y,z and Q quadratic; complete the square in x to obtain (x + 1/2 P)^2 + residual quadratic in y,z; then repeat the process on the residual quadratic (complete square in one variable then the other) until the equation is resolved into a sum/difference of squares and a constant, achieving one of the primitive forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plan: (1) arrange as x^2 + P + Q = 0; (2) complete the square in x producing (x + 1/2 P)^2 + K(y+Jz)^2 + L(... ) = constant; (3) continue completing squares in the remaining variables. In special/exceptional cases where some squares are missing, modify the process (examples are provided). Several worked examples illustrate the step-by-step reduction and identification of conjugate planes, axes, and centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for surface of revolution via adding λ(x^2+y^2+z^2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A surface of second order is a surface of revolution iff there exists a scalar λ such that adding λ(x^2+y^2+z^2) to the quadratic form of the surface yields a complete square (i.e., the expression becomes ± a complete square).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: to the second-order terms add λ(x^2+y^2+z^2) (λ arbitrary) and attempt to choose λ so that the resulting quadratic form is a perfect square. If such λ exists the surface is of revolution; otherwise not. This is justified because the added term corresponds to the square of the distance from the origin and tests for the possibility of two parallel planes through the intersection with a concentric sphere. Examples show solving for λ via algebraic conditions (leads to equations to solve, sometimes a cubic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of cyclic planes / principal planes and axes via cubic for λ
rubrics_metrics.description: To find cyclic (principal) planes and axes of a quadric (when not central), one may determine λ values for which the modified quadratic becomes a complete square; the final equation for λ is a cubic, whose roots give the necessary directions/planes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After adding λ(x^2+y^2+z^2) and forcing the form to be a sum/difference of squares, solve the resulting algebraic conditions for λ. The cubic obtained yields the cyclic planes and principal axes. The text notes this cubic step and demonstrates it in examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling exceptional cases when some squared terms are missing
rubrics_metrics.description: When certain squared terms are absent in the quadratic, the standard completing-the-square sequence must be modified: add and subtract an auxiliary term (with an undetermined coefficient) to create squares, choose the coefficient to make the remainder fit the form, and then proceed to identify the primitive form (often leads to hyperboloid of one sheet, cone, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show adding/subtracting a term (e.g., add/subtract T·x^2 with T chosen to make the residual expressible as squares) and solving for the auxiliary coefficient by equating coefficients; then reduce to a primitive form. The exposition gives worked examples of these exceptional cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of resolving a complete cubic without pre-transforming (alternative to Cardan's transform)
rubrics_metrics.description: A substitution method (introducing auxiliary symmetric quantities y and z and parameter m) yields relations among coefficients, reducing the cubic resolution to solving quadratic equations for auxiliary quantities y and z, and then recovering the root x without transforming the original cubic to eliminate the quadratic term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method begins by assuming a decomposition/substitution (notations in original text) and equating coefficients to derive three relations. By symmetry substitute a and b, derive equations (3) and (4) etc., multiply/divide appropriately to eliminate variables and obtain quadratics solving for y and z; once y and z are found compute m then x. Examples with numerical cubics are provided showing computation (e.g., a^3 - 6a^2 + 18a - 22 = 0). The text emphasizes this method dispenses with the usual preliminary transformation typically required before Cardan's method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural assertion: transformation ordinarily required before Cardan's method
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard practice requires transforming a general cubic to one lacking the second power term before applying Cardan's method; the text asserts 'This transformation must always be effected before Cardan's method of solution can be applied', but presents the preceding method as dispensing with that transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural requirement in the traditional method: eliminate the quadratic term (via Tschirnhaus or shift) prior to applying Cardan; the new method claims to avoid that step. The statement is given as guidance on when the classical transform is necessary vs when the alternative method is applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inradius/exradius formulas for an irregular tetrahedron (relation with face areas and volume)
rubrics_metrics.description: If r is the inradius and r1,r2,r3,r4 are the exradii (spheres each touching one face and the other three produced) of a tetrahedron with face areas A1,A2,A3,A4 and volume V, then r(A1+A2+A3+A4)=3V, and similarly r_i(3S - 2Ai) = 3V (various explicit expressions for r_i in terms of V and face areas are given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From dividing the tetrahedron into four by joining incenter to vertices, the relation r·sum(Ai)=3V follows. The text gives explicit formulae for each exradius and shows examples of resulting expressions like r_i = 3V/(3S - 2Ai) (derivations provided). Use these to compute radii once areas and volume are known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations among reciprocals of radii and perpendiculars from vertices
rubrics_metrics.description: There are multiple algebraic relations connecting reciprocals of the inradius/exradii and the perpendiculars (p1,p2,p3,p4) from vertices to opposite faces, including sum and sum-of-squares relations (e.g., sums like 1/p1 + 1/p2 + 1/p3 + 1/p4 = ... and analogous identities involving r, r_i and products p1p2, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text develops these relations by combining earlier area/volume identities and algebraic manipulations; several sets of symmetric reciprocal relations and identities are listed and can be used to deduce one set of quantities from others. The page shows how to sum, multiply, and combine the base relations to obtain further identities (useful for checks or inversions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula for circumradius of a tetrahedron in terms of rectangles of opposite edges and volume
rubrics_metrics.description: If r1,r2,r3,r4 are the rectangles (products) of pairs of opposite edges and r is half their sum and V the volume, then the radius R of the circumscribing sphere is given by an expression involving these quantities (the page derives an explicit algebraic formula expressing R in terms of the edge-rectangle sums and V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The derivation uses dihedral angle relations, perpendiculars from vertices, and spherical trigonometry; the result is presented in a reduced algebraic form and may be applied to compute the circumradius when the edge products and volume are known. The text gives substitution steps and the final formula (see Prop. III for the full expression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression for the area of the face opposite a solid angle given edge lengths and dihedral angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Given three edges forming a solid angle and the angles between them, the area A4 of the opposite face is given by an explicit formula: A4' = A1'^ + A3'^ + A3* — 2A2A3 cos(β?) — 2A1A3 cos(α) — 2A1A2 cos(γ) (with notation from the text), and simplifies in special cases (e.g., if a dihedral angle is right, A4' = A1' + A2' + A3').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute the given edge lengths and dihedral angles into the formula. The derivation presumes knowledge of the areas Ai and the dihedral angles; the identity is useful to compute one face area from the others and the dihedral geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressions for distances from a vertex to incentre/excentres of the opposite face
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas are given for the distance of the inscribed centre and of exscribed centres of a triangular face from an opposite vertex D (long algebraic expressions involving the sides a,b,c of the face and area terms), with explicit reduced forms and special-case simplifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page provides the algebraic expressions and indicates substitution steps (using previously obtained values of cosines of angles). These distances can be computed by plugging the face side lengths and computed trigonometric quantities into the formulas; several variants and symmetric forms are presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perturbation/planetary-elements method criterion: neglect second-order infinitesimals for perpendicular impulsive disturbances
rubrics_metrics.description: When a disturbing force perpendicular to the orbital plane acts by impulses producing small velocity changes, the change produced in the velocity along the curve by the change of position is a versed sine of a small angle and is an infinitesimal of second order; therefore it may be neglected, and the motion in the orbital plane may be treated as if the plane were fixed for first-order perturbation calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption leads to simpler perturbation equations for the variable elements: one sets certain coordinate variation terms to zero (r is not affected to first order) and proceeds to derive first-order evolution equations for elements (de/dt, da/dt, di/dt, dΩ/dt etc.) with R the perturbing function. The text develops the consequent differential relations and shows how to replace dx, dy by expressions in orbital coordinates to deduce the element variation formulas.
